doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Writing from curiosity and shaping a mature voice for Down Beat
summary: Mandel stresses asking questions out of curiosity and writing a more mature narrator, starting at Down Beat in 1974 and wanting to match Leonard Feather.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Basically getting to know the whole scene as much as you can. I mean you said an important thing there, to write only what you know or feel strongly about.

Well I felt there was so much that I didn’t know anything about, and especially when I was 18 to 25 or something. I mean it was just scratching the surface. I had no idea what this world was that the music was coming out of. And I was interested but I wanted to be very respectful, I was a little shy as outsiders are. I felt like it was okay to ask questions, that’s the journalistic training I had. Ask a question. Find out. You are asking out of

curiosity. It’s genuine and it’s not displaying some sort of awkward egoness or even if it is so what. Nobody’s going to find that out on the page. Whatever the experience is when you do the interview, that’s not what you transmit to the page. You transmit to the page what you learned after the interview, what you’ve come out of it with. And I had ambitions to write fiction so I felt like it was perfectly okay to change the experience, not to change the information, but to change the narrator’s stance. When I got to the page I didn’t have to seem like I was 20 years old. I could seem like I was 25 or 30. And in fact I mean she may have been just flattering me but once I met Marian McPartland at a gig and introduced myself and she said, “Oh I’ve been reading you for several years I thought you were much older.” And again I wanted to be in Down Beat at that time and I started writing for Down Beat in ’74. And I didn’t want to seem like the kid on the block, I wanted to write in a way that seemed like comparably mature to some of the older critics. To Leonard Feather. I didn’t want to seem any less mature or knowledgeable than Leonard, whatever I was writing about. So I didn’t want to come in with a gee whiz attitude. So I thought that was okay to take that liberty as a writer.
